 ## Why Stem
 
 * **Handlebars Syntax**: Remains approachable and compatible with standard frontend tooling.

-=== ADR-0004: Two-Mode Execution Model for SSTI Protection
+=== ADR-0004: Boolean Flag Execution Control for SSTI Protection
 
 Accepted (2026-05-22).
 
 *Context.* Runtime template evaluation introduces Server-Side Template Injection (SSTI) risk. Stem must make the trust boundary explicit and force developers to consciously opt into unsafe behavior.
 
-*Decision.* Implement two execution modes: `:safe` (default) forbids arbitrary Elixir expressions and restricts templates to structured Stem expressions, literals, helpers, and paths; `:permissive` allows arbitrary Elixir code for trusted internal templates. Runtime evaluation APIs (`eval_string/3`, `eval_file/3`) default to `:safe` and require explicit `mode: :permissive` in config or at the call site to enable unrestricted code.
+*Decision.* Control arbitrary Elixir expression execution with the `allow_elixir_expressions` boolean flag. When `false` (default), templates are restricted to structured Stem expressions, literals, helpers, and paths. When `true`, arbitrary Elixir code is permitted. Runtime evaluation APIs (`eval_string/3`, `eval_file/3`) default to `allow_elixir_expressions: false` and require explicit `allow_elixir_expressions: true` in config or at the call site to enable unrestricted code.
 
-*Consequences.* Production templates are protected against SSTI by default. The requirement to explicitly set `mode: :permissive` serves as a visible code-review flag. If a developer needs `:permissive` in production, it signals an architectural flaw—business logic is leaking into the presentation layer and should be refactored into registered helpers or backend services.
+*Consequences.* Production templates are protected against SSTI by default. The requirement to explicitly set `allow_elixir_expressions: true` serves as a visible code-review flag. If a developer needs to enable arbitrary expressions in production, it signals an architectural flaw—business logic is leaking into the presentation layer and should be refactored into registered helpers or backend services.

 == Runtime APIs
 
 Stem provides runtime evaluation APIs for dynamic template compilation:
 
 [source,elixir]
 ----
-# Safe by default — structured Stem expressions only
+# Restricted by default — structured Stem expressions only
 Stem.Unsafe.eval_string("Hello {{name}}", assigns: [name: "Nina"])
 
 # Explicit opt-in for arbitrary Elixir — development/trusted sources only
-Stem.Unsafe.eval_string("{{a + b}}", assigns: [a: 1, b: 2], mode: :permissive)
+Stem.Unsafe.eval_string("{{a + b}}", assigns: [a: 1, b: 2], allow_elixir_expressions: true)
 ----
 
-Always use `:safe` mode (the default) for production templates.
-Only pass `mode: :permissive` when the template source is entirely controlled by your team and arbitrary code execution is necessary.
+Always use `allow_elixir_expressions: false` (the default) for production templates.
+Only pass `allow_elixir_expressions: true` when the template source is entirely controlled by your team and arbitrary code execution is necessary.
 
 For full API reference, see xref:architecture:index.adoc[Architecture] documentation.
 
 == Security Best Practices
 
-* **Always use `:safe` mode in production.** It is the default for a reason.
+* **Always use `allow_elixir_expressions: false` in production.** It is the default for a reason.
 * **Never execute user-generated templates.** If you must, ensure they are validated and safe first.
 * **Use HTML escaping by default.** `{{ expression }}` is escaped; use `{{{ expression }}}` only for trusted content.
 * **Inject all data via `assigns`.** Do not allow templates to read environment variables or access global state.
-* **Register custom helpers instead of relying on `:permissive` mode.** Helper functions keep business logic out of templates.
+* **Register custom helpers instead of enabling arbitrary expressions.** Helper functions keep business logic out of templates.

 Dynamic rendering of untrusted template source at runtime introduces Server-Side Template Injection (SSTI) vulnerabilities, which can lead to arbitrary code execution. @@ -11,16 +11,14 @@ Stem templates act as purely declarative views. They have zero direct access to
 #### Why
 Allowing templates to access global state or execute arbitrary logic violates separation of concerns, tangling generation logic with presentation code. Enforcing a strict boundary keeps templates portable, reusable, and secure against data-exfiltration Server-Side Template Injection (SSTI) attacks. Templates act as exemplars of the desired output with holes where the programmer sticks values — nothing more.
 
-The [[safe-mode]] execution mode enforces this boundary at compile time by forbidding arbitrary Elixir expressions, ensuring templates remain purely declarative.
+The default execution mode (`allow_elixir_expressions: false`) enforces this boundary at compile time by forbidding arbitrary Elixir expressions, ensuring templates remain purely declarative.
 
 #### How
-Fetch all necessary data (API URLs, database records, configuration flags) in the Elixir controller and pass it explicitly via the `assigns` keyword list to your compiled template macros or `Stem.Unsafe` runtime functions. Do not call Elixir system or I/O functions from inside `.stem` files. The compiler's default `mode: :safe` enforces this boundary at compile time.
+Fetch all necessary data (API URLs, database records, configuration flags) in the Elixir controller and pass it explicitly via the `assigns` keyword list to your compiled template macros or `Stem.Unsafe` runtime functions. Do not call Elixir system or I/O functions from inside `.stem` files. The compiler's default `allow_elixir_expressions: false` enforces this boundary at compile time.
